First, a % 3 + b = 7 % 3 + 2 = 1 + 2 = 3, so we enter at case 3. 
case 3: r becomes "X". Now the if: c++ is post-increment – c's current value 0 is used in the 
comparison, then c becomes 1. Since 0 > 0 is false, the && short-circuits and --a is never 
evaluated, so a stays 7. We take the else branch and r becomes "XZ". 
There is no break on case 3, so we fall through to case 2: r becomes "XZQ", then we hit the 
break. 
Finally, r + a + c is string concatenation: "XZQ" + 7 + 1 → "XZQ71".

runs.text: What is output by the code to the right?

questions.explanation:
First, b = a makes b an alias of a. The loop builds a difference array in c: c becomes  
{3, -2, 6, -5, 0}. Note c[4] stays 0 because the loop runs to a.length - 1 
exclusive, so only indices 0–3 are written. 
Then b = c breaks b's alias to a and makes b point at c instead. Now b and c reference the 
same object, while a is independent. 
a[0] += b[0] + c[0]: since b and c are the same array, b[0] and c[0] are both 3. So 
a[0] = 1 + 3 + 3 = 7. 
b[0] = 0: this also sets c[0] to 0 since they're the same array. a is unaffected. 
Final state: a = {7, 4, 2, 8, 3}, b = c = {0, -2, 6, -5, 0}. 
String concatenation: "7" + "0" + "0" + "4" → "7004".

questions.explanation:
The == on Integer objects compares references, not values. Java caches Integer objects for 
values -128 through 127. So a.get(0) == b.get(0) compares two Integer(127) 
objects that are the same cached instance → true. But a.get(1) == b.get(1) compares 
two Integer(128) objects that are distinct heap allocations → false. Indices 0 and 2 
match; 1 and 3 don't. s = 2. 
a.remove(0): removes by index, returns Integer 127. a = [128, 127, 128]. 
a.add(127) appends it. a = [128, 127, 128, 127]. 
a.remove(Integer.valueOf(128)): removes by value — first occurrence only. a = 
[127, 128, 127]. 
b.subList(0, 2).clear(): structural modification through the subList view removes 
indices 0–1. b = [127, 128].

questions.explanation:
https://introcs.cs.princeton.edu/java/11precedence/ 
https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-15.html#jls-15.15 
The Java Language Specification defines associativity through its grammar. In §15.15, unary 
expressions are described as grouping right-to-left (e.g., -~x is parsed as -(~x)), which applies 
to prefix unary operators such as ++x and --x. 
However, the grammar also separates postfix expressions (PostfixExpression) from unary 
expressions. As a result, postfix operators like x++ and x-- associate left-to-right, while prefix 
operators remain right-to-left.
